name: AKBELEK (ow. Melnichenko)
note: Testimony of a Russian breed expert and breeder: <<Ivan Aplevich from Rostov-na-Donu allegedly bought Bassar and Akbelek in Turkmenistan from Ashir Lalakov. However, strangely enough, there are photos of Bassar taken at Lalakov's house, but none of Akbelek. I talked with Ivan Aplevich, who sold Akbelek to Igor Melnichenko of Kirovograd, and I asked him many times where he got Akbelek. At first he told me that he took her from Tajikistan, then that he took her from Mary region in Turkmenistan...he never gave me a precise answer. Besides, he never wanted to tell me who her alleged owner was, because he knows that I can verify it. Ashir Lalakov, who sold Bassar to Ivan Aplevich, told me that he has never known this female dog Akbelek.>>. Given the phenotype of her offspring, there had always been rumours that this female had Saint Bernard blood; however, in early 2026, a Russian vet revealed that her father was Moskow Watchdog Batyr.

name: SYRLON (ow. Levchishin)
note: Testimony of a Russian breed expert and breeder: <<Syrlon had an Uzbek certificate and also another pedigree. It was said that he came from Tajikistan, but it turned out that he was the son of a Moscow Watchdog owned by Alik Ryvin. Savich arranged the mating. Syrlon was born in Gomel, Belarus, to Savich. It was Savich himself who told me these facts. I asked him why he was producing hybrids, and he replied that any means were justified to achieve his goals. Syrlon sired bony, coarse-boned puppies, but they were clearly of a different breed. These are established facts; there are many witnesses. I have also followed the story of the dogs who were born from Syrlon and Sinchuk's Amba: I don't remember their names, but three of them ended up in Kazakhstan, where their bloodline spread, seriously contaminating the breed.>>.

note: According to some long-time enthusiasts of the breed, this dog’s pedigree may have been affected by introgression from dogs belonging to Western breeds. Given this dog’s anatomical characteristics (long thighs, short format index, etc.) - which are indeed atypical for the breed - we share these doubts regarding the authenticity of its pedigree. * Testimony from a Russian breed expert and breeder who has traveled to Turkmenistan dozens of times since the late 1980s: “In 1998, Bayram Kyarizov purchased a male named Elbars from the city of Kazan (Russia), along with his full sister and another male. In the genealogy of Elbars and his full sister there was famous Kakysh Kyarizov's Babur, but, unfortunately, also famous Velikoivanenko's Baron, and thus Great Dane blood. These dogs were widely used for breeding, and it is clear that their descendants have spread throughout much of Turkmenistan. In fact, since the early 2000s, Turkmen dogs have begun to differ from their famous ancestors of the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s. The fact is that today’s Turkmen dogs, especially in the capital region, are significantly different from traditional Turkmen dogs.>>.

note: This male, the son of the famous Stary Moynak, was an extraordinary fighter. Unfortunately, however, his maternal lineage is far from clear and clean.

name: RITSA (Kazakhstan)
note: Testimony of a Kazakh breed expert and breeder: <<Here in our area, there was a dog breeder who started the trend for mixed-breed dogs; he initially bred Caucasian Shepherd Dogs. He mated one of his bitches with a Caucasian Shepherd Dog called Jack, and that’s how Jack 2 was born. Jack 2 was mated with a daughter of the famous Dzhin, who was also a Caucasian Shepherd (though Dzhin certainly also had some Saint Bernard or Moscow Watchdog blood). A daughter of Jack 2 and Dzhin’s daughter was mated with a male Pitbull. From there, a female was sent to a farm where there were mixed-breed and VEO dogs and was mated with an unknown male, and so Dzhon’s mother was born.>>.
